text.p: Insurance companies usually find their way onto the front pages of newspapers for one of two reasons. Either they are involved in a mega deal, or there's a bad news story to tell.

Lloyd's of London is the recent classic example of the latter, with its record losses combined with potential misery for its individual backers. The media latched on to the human interest angle of Names being plunged into penury, many of whom were portrayed as innocent victims.
Now, the European insurance industry may be at the centre of another front-page story which could reveal far greater human tragedy than befell Lloyd's Names.
A lawsuit filed in Manhattan Federal Court on Monday by Holocaust survivors alleges that European insurers cheated them of billions of dollars during the Nazi era.

Allianz, Generali, AGF, RAS and Bavarian Reinsurance are among those mentioned in the U.S. lawsuit. Our enquiries to German insurers last week seemed to catch them unawares, even though the issue first came to light several weeks ago when Generali faced questioning over some of its policies in pre-war eastern Europe.

This week, Allianz and RAS, now a subsidiary of Allianz, confirmed that they have made payments in similar cases in the past. However, no-one appears to know whether the scale of compensation could rise to the billions of dollars mentioned in the U.S. lawsuit.

Perhaps as big an issue for insurers is the way they handle this delicate question, especially in view of the bad publicity Swiss banks attracted last year in connection with the question of Nazi gold.
